analysis.one_liner: Lets tax-exempt charities endorse political candidates without losing their tax exemption.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 41 House Republicans, was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on February 4, 2019 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current tax law, a 501(c)(3) charity — the kind of organization whose donors can deduct gifts, including churches — loses its tax exemption if it backs or attacks a candidate for office. This bill would carve out an exception: a charity could make campaign-related statements, as long as they come in the ordinary course of its normal activities and cost it almost nothing extra. The bill never moved past its referral to the tax-writing committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Churches and other 501(c)(3) organizations, and the people who lead them, would gain a protected way to speak for or against candidates during services, bulletins, and other routine communications without risking their tax-exempt status. Donors would keep deducting gifts to organizations that engage in electoral messaging.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a new subsection to the tax code saying a 501(c)(3) organization cannot lose its exemption solely because of the content of a campaign-related statement made in the ordinary course of its regular activities and costing no more than de minimis incremental expenses.

The protection also applies to the charitable-deduction rules and excise-tax rules that reference the same campaign-intervention ban, so donors and the organization keep the full tax benefits even after political statements.
It applies to tax years ending after enactment, so it would take effect immediately once signed into law.

analysis.who_pays: The general public would bear the cost of charitable dollars — subsidized by tax deductions — flowing into electoral messaging, since donations to charities that campaign would still be deductible. Members of congregations and nonprofit communities would also face campaign advocacy inside spaces, like worship services, they cannot easily leave or opt out of.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and charity members exposed to campaign messaging

drawbacks.text: The bill would let tax-deductible charitable giving subsidize electoral speech, meaning taxpayers effectively help finance campaign messaging funneled through churches and charities.
The bill leaves 'de minimis' expenses undefined in the statute, giving organizations and the IRS no bright line on how much campaign activity the exception covers.

Campaign advocacy delivered inside worship services or mandatory-attendance charity settings is hard for members to avoid or answer, an objection long raised against weakening the ban on charity political intervention.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For churches and nonprofits that want to speak on elections, the bill offers real legal protection, and supporters frame it as free speech for institutions whose members are citizens. The cost is that the political activity would ride on a tax subsidy: donations stay deductible, so the public Treasury shares the bill for campaign messaging, and the line between charity and electoral politics — which also protects charity recipients from being politicized — gets thinner. The narrow 'ordinary course' and 'de minimis' limits keep the change smaller than a full repeal, but the undefined terms leave the scope open.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or brought it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Scalise introduced the bill on February 4, 2019, with Reps. Jody Hice of Georgia and Mike Johnson of Louisiana as original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No action beyond the committee referral is recorded for the rest of the 116th Congress: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

The bill would have added a new subsection (s) to Internal Revenue Code section 501 protecting 501(c)(3) organizations from losing tax-exempt status over campaign-related statements made in the ordinary course of their activities at de minimis expense.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing ban on political campaigning by tax-exempt charities stayed in place, preserving the tax rules as they were; churches and nonprofits that wanted the new freedom, and their allies, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers and existing charity campaign rules

for.name: Steve Scalise
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors.

against.name: Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or committee vote; it sat without action after referral.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 41 cosponsors were House Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic-controlled Ways and Means Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would give congregations a protected way to endorse or oppose candidates from the pulpit without risking tax-exempt status. The benefit to churches would be subsidized by taxpayers, since donor deductions would remain intact even for organizations that campaign.

Any 501(c)(3) — including large advocacy-oriented charities — could fold campaign messaging into its regular communications at little incremental cost while donors keep deducting. That converts a tax-subsidized charitable channel into an electoral one, at the public's expense.
